task.goal: Help first-time library volunteers handle a disagreement about a shared room booking without taking sides prematurely.
hard_constraints: A 45-minute training with role cards and one facilitator.
Do not ask trainees to recount personal conflicts; no legal or disciplinary advice.
Practice must include verifying the booking record, listening to both parties, and knowing when to escalate; assess an unseen scenario individually.
task.available_resources: Fictional booking records and policy excerpt.
task.expected_result: A role-play sequence and actionable escalation check.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A three-gate conversation protocol
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: give novices three gates—hear both accounts, verify the record, then resolve or escalate. Requiring observable evidence before a decision could reduce premature siding, although trainees may follow the sequence mechanically.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce neutrality and the fictional policy; 5–10 the facilitator demonstrates the gates; 10–28 run three six-minute role-play rounds in triads, rotating volunteer and two room users; 28–35 discuss missed gates and repeat difficult moments; 35–43 complete an unseen individual scenario; 43–45 review the escalation check. Nobody recounts personal conflicts.

Role cards give each room user a plausible claim, one relevant detail, and an immediate need. The volunteer receives the booking record and policy excerpt. Each round includes listening to both parties, summarizing each account without endorsing it, checking room/date/time/status in the record, explaining what is established, and proposing only policy-supported next steps.

Actionable escalation check: Is there an immediate safety concern? Follow the excerpt’s safety route. Is the record missing, contradictory, or insufficient? Pause allocation and contact the designated staff member. Does the requested exception exceed volunteer authority, or does disagreement persist after clarification? Escalate with both accounts, verified facts, unresolved questions, and the next update time. Avoid blame, sanctions, and legal conclusions.

Needs: one facilitator, printed role cards, fictional records, and an excerpt specifying volunteer authority and a staff contact route. Assume enough trainees for triads; a pair can alternate the second claimant role. The protocol cannot settle ambiguities the policy leaves unresolved.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use two matched unseen written scenarios, counterbalanced across trainees: one answered before instruction using ordinary judgment, one afterward using the gates. Score record verification, fair hearing, and justified escalation separately. A minimal falsifying result is that protocol users still allocate the room before hearing both claims, or escalate clear routine cases without justification. This small comparison checks usability and immediate performance, not lasting transfer.

DIRECT_FULL.title: An evidence-gap role-play
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: distribute incomplete but compatible information across the two claimants and the booking record. The volunteer can reach a defensible next step only by asking both parties questions and cross-checking the record. This makes impartial listening useful for solving the task, rather than merely a courtesy.

Allocate 45 minutes: 0–5 explain the fictional policy and boundaries; 5–9 demonstrate separating a claim from a verified fact; 9–27 run three six-minute triad rounds with rotating roles; 27–34 reveal the evidence and discuss unsupported assumptions; 34–42 assess an unseen case individually; 42–45 rehearse escalation handoffs. Use fictional situations exclusively.

Each claimant card states what to disclose initially and what to disclose when asked. For example, one person has a confirmation for a different room; the other has the correct room but an outdated time. The booking record establishes current status. Later rounds include a genuinely unresolved discrepancy so that finding more information does not always produce a volunteer-level resolution. Volunteers must hear both accounts and inspect the record in every round.

The escalation check asks: Can I establish the booking from the available record? Does the policy authorize my proposed next step? Can the interaction continue safely and constructively? If any answer is no, use the excerpt’s designated staff route. State what each person reports, what the record confirms, what remains uncertain, and what assistance is needed. Do not assign fault or invent consequences.

Needs: one facilitator, coordinated role cards and records, and a policy excerpt defining authority and escalation contacts. Card preparation requires care: avoid trick wording and ensure information becomes available through reasonable questions. Limits include reading demands and trainees learning to hunt for hidden clues rather than listen naturally.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare one ordinary full-information practice case with one evidence-gap case, counterbalancing order. Then give everyone the same unseen individual case with both accounts and a record available. Check whether trainees identify the decisive discrepancy, acknowledge both accounts, and choose a supported action. The mechanism is weakened if evidence-gap practice produces more guessing or clue-hunting without better verification than ordinary practice.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Pause, compare, and replay decision points
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: rehearse the moment when a volunteer is tempted to decide too early. Short pauses let trainees compare a premature response with an evidence-seeking response, then immediately replay the conversation. The intended change is recognition of decision hazards under pressure; improvement is uncertain until tested without pauses.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce policy and respectful boundaries; 5–10 the facilitator models a rushed decision and invites a replacement line; 10–28 triads complete three six-minute rounds, rotating volunteer and two claimants; 28–34 review decision points; 34–42 complete an unseen individual assessment; 42–45 review the escalation check. All examples are fictional, with no requests for personal experiences.

Role cards introduce distinct pressures: an apparently confident claimant, an urgent request, or two conflicting confirmations. Every round requires listening to both parties and inspecting the booking record. A printed pause marker appears after the opening claims and after record inspection. At each marker the volunteer states what is known, what remains unverified, and the next question or action. The triad briefly compares two responses, selects the policy-supported response, and replays from the marker. The facilitator circulates and corrects substantive misunderstandings.

Actionable escalation check: stop and use the policy’s safety route for immediate safety concerns; seek designated staff when records conflict, authority is insufficient, or disagreement persists after a clear explanation. Give a neutral handoff containing both accounts, verified booking details, the unresolved issue, and the requested staff decision. Avoid disciplinary or legal advice.

Needs: one facilitator, role cards with pause markers, fictional records, and an excerpt defining escalation routes. Assume trainees can use the markers without constant facilitator supervision. Pauses may make practice easier than real service, so the final assessment removes them.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Have trainees first answer a brief unseen case without prompts, then assess a matched unseen case individually after rehearsal. Require their opening response, record checks, summaries of both accounts, and escalation decision. Compare against the simple pretraining response. A falsifying signal is successful prompted replay followed by premature siding or unsupported decisions when markers disappear; that would suggest dependence on rehearsal cues rather than transferable judgment.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Reverse the claimants, preserve the facts
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: replay the same dispute after swapping the claimants’ presentation styles while preserving every booking fact. A confident, familiar-sounding claimant becomes hesitant; the other becomes assertive. Comparing the volunteer’s responses makes reliance on confidence or apparent familiarity visible. The intended change is a more stable judgment based on verified facts and both accounts, rather than personal impressions. This differs from simply rotating practice roles: the controlled reversal is the teaching device.

Use 45 minutes: 0–6 introduce the fictional policy and boundaries; 6–10 explain role cards and neutral opening language; 10–28 run three six-minute triad cycles, rotating the volunteer. Each cycle includes a short encounter, a replay with claimant styles reversed, and comparison. Use 28–33 to discuss which responses changed and why; 33–42 for an unseen individual assessment; 42–45 for the escalation check. Use fictional disputes only; offer no legal or disciplinary advice.

Both versions require the volunteer to hear each party, summarize their accounts, and verify room, date, time, and booking status against the record. Cards specify identical substantive information across versions, disclosed without requiring clever questions. Respectful listening should remain consistent even when delivery changes.

Escalation check: follow the excerpt’s safety route for immediate danger; contact designated staff if records remain contradictory, a requested action exceeds volunteer authority, or disagreement persists after explanation. Hand over both accounts, verified details, the unresolved question, and the assistance needed.

Needs: one facilitator, paired role cards, fictional records, and an excerpt defining authority and staff contacts. Triads must manage timing independently. Style changes should avoid identity stereotypes. Repetition may itself improve performance, and trainees may recognize the lesson without transferring it to service.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In a small pilot, give some triads a style-reversal replay and others an identical replay, with equal practice time. Everyone then answers the same unseen scenario individually, stating their opening response, questions for both parties, record checks, and escalation decision. Compare premature allocation and unsupported reliance on confidence. The mechanism is weakened if reversal practice produces no improvement over ordinary repetition, or merely makes trainees favor the quieter claimant. This checks immediate transfer, not durable behavior.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Learn the boundary through contrasting cases
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: teach volunteers to distinguish cases they can handle from cases requiring staff by comparing closely matched disputes whose decisive difference is authority or evidence quality. Contrast can expose the actual escalation boundary: a clear record supports one action, while an unresolved discrepancy or unauthorized exception requires staff. This aims to prevent both premature decisions and automatic escalation of every disagreement.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce the fictional policy and boundaries; 5–11 compare two short case files differing in one decisive fact; 11–29 run three six-minute triad role-plays, rotating volunteer and two claimants; 29–34 compare decisions against the excerpt; 34–42 assess an unseen scenario individually; 42–45 rehearse a staff handoff. All situations are fictional; do not solicit personal conflicts or provide legal or disciplinary advice.

Prepare three practice packets: a routine case with a clear current booking, a matched case with conflicting current records, and a clear booking accompanied by an exception request outside volunteer authority. Role cards give both claimants reasonable concerns. In every encounter, volunteers listen to both parties and verify room, date, time, and status before choosing a next step. Trainees explain which specific fact or policy provision permits action or requires escalation; politeness alone does not count as a justified decision.

Actionable escalation check: Is there an immediate safety concern requiring the excerpt’s safety route? Can the booking be established? Is the proposed action within volunteer authority? Does disagreement persist after clarification? For unresolved evidence, insufficient authority, or persistent disagreement, contact designated staff and report both accounts, confirmed details, and the decision needed.

Needs: one facilitator, coordinated role cards and fictional records, and a policy excerpt with explicit authority boundaries and contacts. Assume triads can run from printed directions. Contrasts must be realistic and unambiguous; overly tidy examples could teach brittle rules that fail on mixed cases.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot contrasting-case instruction against an equal-length explanation using unrelated examples, keeping role-play time equal. Give each trainee one unseen case combining a clear booking with an unauthorized exception request. Individually assess whether they hear both accounts, verify the record, and distinguish confirmed booking facts from the staff decision required. A falsifying result is equally frequent unsupported allocation or blanket escalation without identifying the authority boundary. A single small pilot offers only preliminary evidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Build a shared account before proposing action
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: use a visible, three-column worksheet—“Party A reports,” “Party B reports,” and “Record confirms”—to keep claims separate from established facts. Before proposing action, the volunteer reads back the account and invites each claimant to correct their own entry. Externalizing the information could reduce memory errors and make accidental endorsement visible. Agreement about who should use the room is not required.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce the fictional policy and boundaries; 5–10 demonstrate the worksheet; 10–28 run three six-minute triad rounds, rotating volunteer and two room users; 28–34 review worksheets and practice neutral corrections; 34–42 assess an unseen scenario individually; 42–45 review escalation. Discuss fictional cases only; solicit no personal conflicts and give no legal or disciplinary advice.

Role cards give each claimant a booking claim and a practical concern. The volunteer hears both accounts, records them without treating either as verified, and checks room, date, time, and status against the fictional record. Each claimant checks their own summary. Corrections remain attributed unless independently confirmed. The volunteer then explains which next step the policy supports.

Escalation check: use the excerpt’s safety route for immediate safety concerns. Contact designated staff when booking evidence remains unresolved, the requested action exceeds volunteer authority, or disagreement continues after clarification. Hand over both accounts, verified details, remaining uncertainty, and the assistance needed. Never treat a claimant’s refusal to endorse the worksheet as proof against them.

Needs: one facilitator, role cards, fictional records, a policy excerpt specifying authority and contacts, and blank worksheets. Assume a manageable group working in self-directed triads. Writing may slow conversation; concise notes and reading entries aloud reduce that burden. The worksheet cannot establish whether the underlying record is accurate.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In a small pilot, give some triads the worksheet and others ordinary blank paper, with identical instructions and practice time. Assess everyone individually on the same unseen packet containing two accounts and a booking record. Score whether they distinguish claims from verified facts, represent both parties accurately, and justify action or escalation. The mechanism is weakened if worksheets produce equally frequent claim-as-fact errors, or accurate notes followed by unsupported allocation. This checks immediate performance, not durable transfer.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Practice repairing a premature commitment
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: teach a specific recovery skill for when a volunteer has already appeared to take sides. Rehearsing an explicit correction may make it easier to withdraw an unsupported commitment instead of defending it. The intended outcome is recoverable judgment: a novice notices the mistake, acknowledges it, and resumes fair inquiry. Whether that transfers beyond rehearsal remains uncertain.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 explain the fictional policy and boundaries; 5–10 demonstrate a repair; 10–28 complete three six-minute triad rounds with rotating volunteers; 28–34 discuss repair language and repeat weak attempts; 34–42 assess an unseen case individually; 42–45 rehearse escalation. Use fictional material exclusively, without personal-conflict disclosures or legal or disciplinary advice.

Each round begins with a printed statement attributed to the volunteer, such as “I said you could have the room before checking the booking.” Trainees do not need to invent or perform the initial mistake. Their task is to repair it: “I spoke before checking the information. I need to hear both accounts and verify the booking before explaining the next step.” They then listen to both claimants, summarize each account, and inspect room, date, time, and booking status. Role cards let a claimant ask whether the earlier promise still stands. The volunteer must explain the correction without blaming either person or promising an unauthorized remedy.

Escalation check: follow the excerpt’s safety route for immediate safety concerns; contact designated staff for unresolved records, requests beyond volunteer authority, or continuing disagreement after clarification. Include the earlier commitment in the handoff alongside both accounts, verified facts, and the decision needed.

Needs: one facilitator, role cards, fictional records, and an excerpt defining authority and staff contacts. Assume triads can follow printed timing. Model the correction prominently so trainees do not mistake the opening error for acceptable practice. Repair must not become a substitute for careful initial handling.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare recovery rehearsal with equal-time practice that begins before any commitment, using the same policy and verification requirements. Give each trainee an unseen individual scenario in which a volunteer’s earlier assurance conflicts with newly available information. Ask for their next words, checks, and escalation decision. Recovery practice is not supported if trainees preserve the unsupported promise, blame a claimant, or retract it without hearing both parties and checking the record. Include a fresh-start item to inspect whether rehearsing mistakes inadvertently normalizes premature commitments.

EXPAND.title: Find the smallest authorized next step
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: teach volunteers to establish only the facts needed for an authorized next step, without deciding who caused the disagreement. Working backward from a useful outcome can prevent unnecessary investigation and blame. Unlike the prior three-gate protocol, this route explicitly teaches when enough information has been gathered.

Prepare claimant role cards, fictional records, and a policy excerpt stating volunteer authority and staff contacts. Use 45 minutes: 0–6 introduce the policy and demonstrate a sufficient-information decision; 6–10 prepare roles; 10–28 run three six-minute triad rounds with rotating volunteers; 28–34 discuss unnecessary questions; 34–42 assess an unseen scenario individually; 42–45 review handoffs. Use fictional cases exclusively, with no personal disclosures or legal or disciplinary advice.

In each round, the volunteer hears both accounts, checks the record’s room, date, time and status, and identifies the immediate request. They ask only questions that could change an authorized next step. A clear record permits the routine action specified in the excerpt. A consequential discrepancy or request beyond volunteer authority requires staff assistance. Volunteers need not establish whose memory failed before helping.

Escalation check: immediate safety concern—use the excerpt’s safety route; unresolved booking fact that changes access—contact designated staff; requested exception outside authority—request a staff decision. While waiting, explain the uncertainty and the next contact or update arrangement without promising access. Resume only when sufficient information or staff direction arrives.

Prerequisites are a policy that distinguishes routine actions from exceptions and records with identifiable decisive fields. The limit is that trainees may stop questioning too soon; both accounts and record verification remain mandatory.
EXPAND.experiment: The facilitator owns a first trial using matched cases for this approach and the prior three-gate protocol, with order varied across trainees. Individually assess an unseen case by requesting the opening response, record checks, next action and handoff if needed. Compare supported next steps, premature siding and questions asked. Stop using the shortcut if trainees omit either account, miss a consequential record discrepancy, or gain speed by transferring avoidable work to staff. No improvement means equal or worse decisions without a meaningful reduction in unnecessary questioning.

EXPAND.title: Learn the authority boundary through contrasting cases
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: teach action versus handoff through closely contrasting examples and immediate explanatory feedback. Novices may know how to listen and verify yet still misjudge whether they have authority to act. This route trains that distinction directly, rather than relying on the prior protocol’s escalation checklist to produce calibrated judgment.

Prepare role-card sets and records for a close pair: both have a clear booking, but one asks for its ordinary policy-supported use and the other asks for an exception requiring staff approval. Add an unfamiliar case involving an unresolved record discrepancy. The excerpt must explicitly support these distinctions; otherwise the facilitator cannot teach a defensible boundary.

Allocate 45 minutes: 0–6 explain authority and contact routes; 6–11 trainees individually choose actions for the close pair and receive policy-based feedback; 11–29 run three six-minute triad role-plays with rotating volunteers; 29–34 compare the decisions; 34–42 individually assess three unseen short cases—a new close pair and one unfamiliar case; 42–45 review corrections. All material is fictional; do not solicit personal conflicts or give legal or disciplinary advice.

Every role-play requires hearing and neutrally summarizing both parties, checking room/date/time/status in the record, and identifying the precise policy permission or missing permission. The volunteer then acts within authority or requests the designated staff decision. A handoff states both accounts, confirmed facts, the unresolved question and the assistance requested. During a wait, communicate the contact attempt and update arrangement; follow the excerpt’s safety route if needed.

The actionable check is: does the record establish the relevant booking, and does the excerpt authorize this particular action? A missing consequential fact or permission triggers staff assistance. This method may teach narrow pattern matching, making the unfamiliar assessment essential.
EXPAND.experiment: The facilitator compares this lesson with an equally timed three-gate lesson using the same records and individual assessment. Score routine action, justified handoff and premature siding separately, alongside decision time. Stop the trial if apparent improvement comes from escalating nearly everything or confidently applying the close-pair answer to the unfamiliar case. The mechanism adds no value if boundary choices are no better after accounting for lesson time and unnecessary staff referrals.

EXPAND.title: Make a shared, correctable account visible
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: use a shared written account to expose misunderstandings before they become competing accusations. A volunteer can privately understand both claims while each claimant still believes the other has been favored. Making claims, record facts and unresolved questions visible gives both parties a way to correct the account without requiring agreement about fault.

Resources are role cards, fictional records, the policy excerpt and a blank reverse side of each record divided into three areas: ‘Each person reports,’ ‘Record confirms,’ and ‘Still unresolved.’ No additional facilitator is needed. Assume participants can read the sheet or hear it read aloud; never require signatures or agreement.

Use 45 minutes: 0–6 demonstrate a neutral shared account; 6–10 explain roles and policy boundaries; 10–28 run three six-minute triad rounds, rotating volunteer and both claimants; 28–34 discuss corrections; 34–42 complete an unseen individual assessment; 42–45 rehearse handoffs. Use only fictional disputes, without personal-conflict recounting or legal or disciplinary advice.

The volunteer hears both parties, records their claims separately, verifies room/date/time/status, then reads the sheet aloud and invites factual corrections. A disputed claim remains attributed to its speaker; agreement does not turn it into a verified fact. The volunteer explains the policy-supported next step using the confirmed information.

Escalate through the excerpt’s route for safety concerns, consequential record uncertainty, requests beyond authority or continuing disagreement requiring staff support. Pass the corrected sheet to staff and explain the next update arrangement. Staff clarification is added as a new fact before service resumes.

Compared with the prior evidence-gap approach, the causal lever is shared understanding rather than eliciting hidden information. Its limits are writing time, literacy demands and the possibility that a polished sheet gives uncertain claims undue credibility.
EXPAND.experiment: The facilitator trials one shared-sheet round and one equally timed oral three-gate round, varying order. Claimant cards include a plausible detail the volunteer might misstate. Count uncorrected misstatements, premature allocations and time spent documenting; then assess an unseen case individually, requiring a completed account and next action. Stop if documentation crowds out listening or presents disputed claims as facts. No improvement is shown if accuracy and supported decisions match oral practice while handling time increases.

EXPAND.title: Expose credibility bias by swapping claimant cues
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: hold the booking evidence constant while reversing which claimant sounds confident, familiar or hesitant. Seeing a judgment change when only these cues change can teach novices to separate perceived credibility from booking entitlement. The prior pause-and-replay route interrupts rushed decisions; this route specifically tests whether socially persuasive cues are driving them.

Prepare two versions of a fictional dispute with identical substantive claims, records and policy. In the second, swap only mild delivery cues between claimants. Avoid demographic stereotypes, shouting or demanding acting. Prepare a third dispute with different booking facts. The policy excerpt must specify volunteer authority and staff routes.

Allocate 45 minutes: 0–6 introduce the policy and fictional exercise; 6–10 demonstrate neutral acknowledgment; 10–28 conduct three six-minute triad rounds with rotating volunteers; 28–34 compare the first two versions and discuss evidence-based reasons for decisions; 34–42 assess an unseen scenario individually; 42–45 review escalation. Trainees never recount personal conflicts, and the facilitator gives no legal or disciplinary advice.

During each round the volunteer hears both parties, summarizes both accounts and verifies room/date/time/status before explaining an authorized action. Claimants reveal all relevant information through ordinary conversation; there are no hidden clues. Trainees record which specific facts support their response. The third round checks whether attention transfers to changed evidence.

Escalation check: use the excerpt’s safety route for immediate safety concerns; contact designated staff for consequential record conflicts, exceptions outside volunteer authority or persistent disagreement. Handoffs contain both accounts, verified facts and the unresolved decision. Communicate the contact attempt and update arrangement, then follow staff direction when received.

This requires consistent role-card delivery and a facilitator who distinguishes interpersonal warmth from evidence. Repeated evidence may reveal the exercise’s purpose, so practice consistency alone cannot establish transfer.
EXPAND.experiment: The facilitator compares swapped-cue practice with equally timed pause-and-replay practice. Assign different unseen individual versions containing identical evidence but reversed confidence cues. Assess supported decisions, whether both accounts were heard and whether record facts were checked; also note hesitation or unnecessary referrals. Stop if trainees become dismissive of distressed or confident claimants. The mechanism is unsupported if decisions remain cue-sensitive, or any reduction in bias is accompanied by worse listening or more unsupported escalation.

EXPAND.title: Three gates with an owned handoff
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: the three-gate conversation protocol. Preserve hearing both accounts, verifying the booking record, and choosing an authorized action or escalation. Change the handoff: contacting staff does not itself transfer responsibility. The volunteer remains the contact for both parties until the designated staff member accepts the case; after interruption, they resume from the last verified fact rather than restart or assume resolution. This closes a consequential gap when a referral receives no response.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce the fictional policy; 5–10 demonstrate the gates and an unanswered referral; 10–28 run three six-minute triad rounds with rotating volunteer and two claimant roles; 28–34 discuss and replay interrupted handoffs; 34–42 assess unseen cases individually; 42–45 correct errors. Each round requires hearing and neutrally summarizing both accounts and checking room, date, time and booking status. Claimant cards supply plausible competing accounts. Include a routine booking, an exception request, and conflicting records.

Escalation check: immediate safety concern—use the excerpt’s safety route; consequential unresolved booking fact, action outside volunteer authority, or continuing disagreement—contact designated staff. Relay both accounts, verified facts, the unresolved decision and assistance requested. Explain who has been contacted and when an update will be given. Until acceptance, the volunteer owns communication, without promising access. If contact fails, use only the excerpt’s backup route or waiting arrangement. If none is specified, state that a staff decision remains pending and make no unsupported allocation. Staff acceptance transfers the decision; the volunteer communicates the authorized outcome and re-escalates if it cannot be implemented.

Needs: one facilitator, role cards, fictional records and an excerpt identifying authority and contact routes. The facilitator must check these prerequisites before training; absent a backup route, teach the pending-status fallback explicitly. All examples are fictional; no personal-conflict recounting or legal or disciplinary advice. Added communication takes time, but may prevent abandoned referrals; actual benefit is untested.
EXPAND.experiment: The facilitator runs a first cohort trial against the original three-gate procedure using matched practice cases, varying order across triads. Simulate staff nonresponse in one round without adding a second facilitator: a sealed response card says whether the referral was accepted. Individually assess three unseen short cases within eight minutes: a clearly authorized routine action, a closely matched exception requiring staff, and an unfamiliar discrepancy with an interrupted referral. Score both-party listening, specified record checks, premature siding, justified action or escalation, and responsibility before acceptance. Compare handling time and unnecessary waiting as well as decisions. Stop and reteach if trainees mistake an attempted referral for acceptance or promise access without authority. If ownership improves only by delaying clear routine cases, simplify the added step to escalated cases.

EXPAND.title: Contrasting authority cases with an applicability boundary
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: learn the authority boundary through contrasting cases. Preserve close examples, policy-based feedback, mandatory listening and record checks. Change the working decision: before applying a familiar example, the volunteer checks whether its policy condition actually holds. A materially different booking type or an omitted exception rule is an unresolved applicability question, not permission to extend the example. This addresses confident but unsupported transfer to unfamiliar cases.

Use 45 minutes: 0–6 introduce the excerpt and contact routes; 6–11 individually judge a close pair and receive explanatory feedback; 11–29 complete three six-minute triad role-plays with rotating volunteer and claimant roles; 29–34 compare which policy conditions supported each decision; 34–42 assess unseen cases individually; 42–45 correct errors. Role cards cover ordinary use, a closely matched exception, and a case whose relevant condition is not covered by the excerpt. Each volunteer hears and summarizes both accounts, verifies room/date/time/status, and explains which provision supports the particular next action.

Actionable check: does the record establish the relevant booking, and does an applicable provision authorize this action? If yes, perform the routine action. If a consequential fact or applicability condition remains unresolved, seek the designated staff decision rather than inventing a rule. Use the safety route for immediate safety concerns and staff support for persistent disagreement. Handoffs include both accounts, confirmed facts and the exact unresolved question. The volunteer owns communication until staff accepts; an interrupted referral remains pending and follows the excerpt’s backup route. If no backup is provided, explain the pending decision without promising access. If the authorized action fails, report the failure to staff rather than improvising an exception.

Needs: one facilitator, coordinated role cards and records, and an excerpt with at least one clear routine permission, one staff-only exception and contact instructions. The facilitator validates the close pair against the excerpt beforehand; if the distinction is unsupported, replace the pair or teach it as unresolved. Use fictional disputes only, with no personal disclosures or legal or disciplinary advice. The extra applicability question may slow decisions or increase referrals; its value depends on reducing unsupported action without making routine cases seem ambiguous.
EXPAND.experiment: The facilitator compares the revised lesson with the original contrasting-case lesson in a bounded first trial using equivalent materials and equal time. Individually assess a new close pair on opposite sides of the authority boundary and one unfamiliar case where a familiar rule’s prerequisite is absent. Require an opening response, both-account summaries, record checks, the supporting policy condition, next action and any handoff recovery. Compare premature siding, supported routine action, justified escalation, decision time and unnecessary staff referrals. Stop using the added boundary if trainees routinely refuse clearly authorized actions; revise its wording before another trial. Evidence for benefit requires fewer unsupported extensions without a corresponding increase in avoidable referrals; no such result is assumed.

EXPAND.title: Repair an inherited decision before it hardens
EXPAND.proposal:
New mechanism: train explicit correction of an unsupported decision already communicated. Prior routes largely begin with a volunteer who has not yet taken a position. This route removes that starting assumption: a volunteer may inherit a confident statement from an earlier interaction and feel obliged to defend it. Practicing a brief correction can reopen fact-finding before that statement becomes a commitment to one party.

Use 45 minutes: 0–6 introduce the fictional policy and correction language; 6–10 demonstrate an inherited unsupported allocation; 10–28 run three six-minute triad rounds with rotating volunteer and two claimants; 28–34 discuss and replay repairs; 34–42 assess unseen cases individually; 42–45 review corrections and escalation. Each role set includes a printed opening statement such as ‘You were told this room was definitely yours,’ both claimant accounts, the booking record and the policy excerpt. The statement may prove correct or incorrect, so trainees must investigate rather than automatically reverse it.

The volunteer acknowledges the prior statement without endorsing it: ‘That was stated before the booking details were checked. I need to hear both accounts and verify the record before confirming the next step.’ They hear and neutrally summarize both parties, check room/date/time/status, then explain what the evidence and policy support. If the earlier statement was mistaken, correct it plainly and give the authorized next step without blaming its speaker. If correct, confirm it with its factual basis.

Escalate safety concerns through the excerpt’s safety route; refer consequential record uncertainty, exceptions beyond authority, or persistent disagreement to designated staff. The volunteer retains responsibility for communication until staff accepts, carries both accounts and verified facts into the handoff, and uses the stated backup route after interruption. If no backup exists, communicate that the decision remains pending without promising access. If the correction is rejected or the authorized action fails, request staff assistance rather than argue or invent concessions.

Needs: one facilitator, fictional role cards and records, and a policy excerpt defining authority and contacts. Assume the practice begins before any consequential room-use change; if reversing an action would exceed volunteer authority, staff must decide it. No personal-conflict recounting or legal or disciplinary advice. Correction can undermine confidence if overused, so the volunteer corrects only the unsupported certainty and verifies before changing the outcome. Transfer beyond rehearsed wording remains uncertain.
EXPAND.experiment: The facilitator compares one inherited-decision practice round with an equally timed clean-start three-gate round, varying order. Within the individual assessment, use three unseen short cases: an earlier claim supported by a routine booking, a closely matched request requiring a staff exception, and an unfamiliar contradictory record. Score whether trainees hear both parties, verify the record, avoid defending or automatically reversing the earlier claim, and choose a justified action or escalation. Also assess repair clarity, handoff ownership and added handling time against ordinary three-gate practice. Stop and reteach if trainees retract valid bookings without verification, blame the earlier speaker, or attempt unauthorized reversal. Retain the mechanism only if it improves recovery from inherited certainty without degrading decisions in clear cases; a first trial establishes usability, not durable transfer.
